title: Advanced Generics
summary: Combine constraints, understand in and out, and write maths that works for every number type.

steps.title: Combining constraints
body: A constraint is a promise about `T`. The more you promise, the more the method body is allowed to do with a `T`.
static T CreateNamed<T>(string name) where T : class, INamed, new()
T item = new T();     // allowed because of new()
item.Name = name;     // allowed because of INamed
Several constraints are separated by commas, and the order is fixed:
1. `class` or `struct` (or a base class) comes first
With two type parameters, each gets its own `where` clause:
static TValue GetOrCreate<TKey, TValue>(Dictionary<TKey, TValue> map, TKey key)

steps.prompt: Match each constraint to the promise it makes about `T`.
pairs: has a public constructor with no parameters
two values can be compared with `CompareTo`

steps.title: Spawn
prompt: A warehouse needs to create numbered items of any kind. The harness already has:
interface IEntity { int Id { get; set; } }
class Crate : IEntity { public int Id { get; set; } }
class Pallet : IEntity { public int Id { get; set; } }
Write `static List<T> Spawn<T>(int count)` that creates `count` new `T` objects with `Id` set to 1, 2, 3 and so on, and returns them in that order.
`Spawn<Crate>(3)` returns three different crates with ids 1, 2, 3.
You will need two constraints on `T` to make the body compile.
starter: // TODO: add the constraints, then create the items
solution: static List<T> Spawn<T>(int count) where T : IEntity, new()
template: Dojo.Eq("Their ids are 1, 2, 3", "1, 2, 3", string.Join(", ", crates.Select(c => c.Id)));
Dojo.Check("They are three different objects", crates.Distinct().Count() == 3, "Create a new T for every item.");
Dojo.Eq("Spawn<Pallet>(5) ends with id 5", 5, Spawn<Pallet>(5).Select(p => p.Id).LastOrDefault());
interface IEntity { int Id { get; set; } }
class Crate : IEntity { public int Id { get; set; } }
class Pallet : IEntity { public int Id { get; set; } }
hints: To write `new T()` the compiler needs the `new()` constraint. To write `item.Id` it needs `IEntity`.
The signature is `static List<T> Spawn<T>(int count) where T : IEntity, new()`.
Loop `i` from 1 to `count`: `T item = new T(); item.Id = i; items.Add(item);`

steps.title: Generic interfaces
body: Interfaces can have type parameters too. `IEnumerable<T>`, `IComparable<T>` and `IEquatable<T>` are ones you have used already.
A class that implements it has two choices. It can **fill in** the type:
or **stay generic** and pass its own `T` along:
One class can even implement the same interface twice with different types, such as `IParser<int>` and `IParser<decimal>`.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so that a `WeightParser` can be used wherever an `IParser<double>` is expected.
steps.explain: The class fills in `T` with `double`, so its `Parse` must return `double`.

steps.title: Covariance: out
body: Every `Cat` is an `Animal`. Is every `IEnumerable<Cat>` an `IEnumerable<Animal>`? Yes:

This works because `IEnumerable` is declared as `IEnumerable<out T>`. The word `out` says: *`T` only ever comes out of this interface*. If all you can do is take animals out, a box of cats is a perfectly good box of animals. This is called **covariance**.
`List<T>` has no `out`, and for a good reason:
List<Animal> animals = cats;     // does NOT compile...
animals.Add(new Dog());          // ...because this would put a dog among the cats
`IReadOnlyList<out T>` and `Func<out TResult>` are covariant too.
> **Tip:** Variance only works for reference types. `IEnumerable<int>` is not an `IEnumerable<object>`.

steps.prompt: `Cat` and `Dog` both derive from `Animal`. Why does C# refuse `List<Animal> pets = new List<Cat>();`?
options: Because `pets.Add(new Dog())` would then put a dog into a list of cats
Because a `Cat` is not really an `Animal` at run time
Because generic types can never be converted to each other
Because `List<T>` is a class, and only interfaces can be assigned
steps.explain: A list lets you put values *in*, so treating a list of cats as a list of animals would be unsafe. A read-only view such as `IEnumerable<Animal>` has no way in, so it is allowed.

steps.title: Contravariance: in
body: The opposite direction exists too. Something that can **consume** any `Animal` can certainly consume a `Cat`:
`Action` is declared as `Action<in T>`. The word `in` says: *`T` only ever goes in*. This is **contravariance**, and it runs from base to derived.
| Keyword | `T` appears as | Conversion allowed | Examples |
You can use both words on your own interfaces:
interface ISink<in T> { void Accept(T item); }

steps.prompt: `Cat` derives from `Animal`. `feedAnimal` is an `Action<Animal>` and `feedCat` is an `Action<Cat>`. Does each line compile?
steps.explain: Producers (`out`) convert from derived to base. Consumers (`in`) convert from base to derived. `List<T>` does both, so it converts neither way. And `int` is a value type, so variance does not apply to it.

steps.title: default(T) and generic maths
body: Inside a generic method you sometimes need *a* value of type `T` before you have one. `default(T)` gives the zero value of whatever `T` turns out to be: `0` for numbers, `false` for `bool`, `null` for reference types.

For years there was no way to write `a + b` for a generic `T`, because an interface could not describe an operator. Now it can. An interface may declare **static abstract** members, and `System.Numerics` uses that to describe numbers:
static T Total<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
T sum = T.Zero;                 // a static member, called on the type parameter
`int`, `double`, `decimal` and every other built-in number implement `INumber<T>`, so one method serves them all. To turn an ordinary `int` into a `T`, use `T.CreateChecked(5)`.

steps.explain: The default of a number is `0`, of a `bool` is `false` (printed as `False`), and of a reference type or a nullable value type is `null`.

steps.title: Average of anything
prompt: Write `static T Average<T>(IEnumerable<T> values)` that works for **any number type**.
- It returns the sum divided by the count, using `T`'s own division. So for `int` it is an integer division: the average of 2, 4, 9 is `5`.
- For an empty sequence it returns zero.
Do the adding yourself, without LINQ's `Sum` or `Average`.
starter: static T Average<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
// TODO: add the values up, count them, divide
solution: static T Average<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>
template: Dojo.Eq("Average of the ints 2, 4, 9 is 5", 5, Average(new[] { 2, 4, 9 }));
Dojo.Eq("Average of the doubles 1.5, 2.5 is 2.0", 2.0, Average(new[] { 1.5, 2.5 }));
Dojo.Eq("Average of the decimals 2, 3 is 2.5", 2.5m, Average(new[] { 2m, 3m }));
Dojo.Eq("Average of one long is that long", 7L, Average(new List<long> { 7L }));
Dojo.Eq("Average of no ints is 0", 0, Average(new List<int>()));

forbid.message: Does not call LINQ's Sum or Average

hints: Start with `T sum = T.Zero;` and an `int count = 0;`, then loop.
You cannot divide a `T` by an `int`. Convert the count first: `T.CreateChecked(count)`.
